technical_resources.lighting: Diffuse, even illumination across the scene with warm, golden-brown tones dominating. Light appears to come from above and slightly from the left, creating subtle shadows beneath figures and architectural elements. The sky transitions from pale cream to soft blue-gray in the distance.

Figures are rendered in dark brown and black skin tones contrasted against white head wraps and garments. Accent colors include blue (jackets, garments), orange/red (breeches, garments), yellow (garments), and green (one garment). Architectural elements use warm browns and tans. The distant landscape employs pale greens and blues.
technical_resources.composition_notes: Horizontal frieze-like arrangement with figures distributed across the foreground plane. Two buildings frame the composition on left and right. The middle ground shows a river or water feature with distant plantation buildings and trees in the background. The composition emphasizes a linear, processional quality with figures arranged in a shallow depth plane. The central area is occupied by the most dynamically posed figures, while peripheral figures are more static. The arrangement suggests a narrative sequence or simultaneous activity rather than a unified action.

identified_elements.generic_description: Percussion instrument held between knees by a seated musician, struck with sticks or bones

identified_elements.confidence_note: The Old Plantation Painting.pdf notes that 'Some scholars saw it as the gudugudu, a particular type of African drum.' The source notes that 'The lower curves of the items that the two women are holding appear to suggest rounded objects of some weight' and that the 'difference in left- and right-hand positions on the ends of the items suggests an inequality of weight distribution from end to end, thus lending more credibility to the shegureh theory.'

stage_3_narrative.description: This watercolor on paper, titled 'The Old Plantation' and attributed to John Rose (c. 1785–1795), depicts a secular scene of communal leisure and musical performance set on a plantation in what is now Beaufort County, South Carolina. The composition is organized as a horizontal frieze with sixteen figures of African descent distributed across the foreground plane, flanked by two wooden structures (likely plantation outbuildings or slave quarters) on the left and right. The scene is set in an open yard or courtyard area adjacent to a river visible in the middle ground, with distant plantation buildings and trees visible across the water in the background. The painting documents a moment of collective music-making and dance, with figures engaged in or observing the performance of African-derived musical instruments and movement practices. The central focus is occupied by a male figure (fig_09) in dynamic forward-bent posture holding a long staff or walking cane, positioned as if leading or participating in a dance. Flanking this central figure are two women (figs_08 and fig_10) who appear to be dancing or moving with what the reference material identifies as African musical instruments—gourd rattles enclosed in nets (shegureh or shegurch). To the right, a standing male figure (fig_13) plays a four-stringed banjo with a body that may consist of a hollow gourd or calabash, an instrument documented in 18th-century colonial contexts as having African origins. Another male figure (fig_14) holds what appears to be a percussion instrument (possibly a gudugudu or pottery vessel idiophone) positioned between the knees and struck with sticks or bones. Additional figures (figs_01, fig_02, fig_04–fig_07, fig_11, fig_12, fig_14–fig_16) stand in various poses around the periphery, some appearing to observe or participate in the musical gathering. The composition emphasizes the collective nature of the activity, with children (figs_03, fig_05, fig_10) interspersed among adults, suggesting a family or community gathering. The scene is rendered in warm earth tones (ochre, tan, beige) with figures depicted in dark brown and black skin tones contrasted against white head wraps and garments in blue, orange, yellow, and white. The lighting is diffuse and even, with the sky transitioning from pale cream to soft blue-gray in the distance. The painting documents material culture associated with African-descended populations in colonial North America, including head ties (head kerchiefs) worn by most figures, layered garments combining European and African-derived clothing practices, and musical instruments of documented African origin. The reference material on African and Afrodescendant cultural practices in colonial Latin America and North America indicates that such communal music-making and dance gatherings, incorporating African musical instruments, rhythmic practices, and movement vocabularies, were significant expressions of cultural continuity and social cohesion among enslaved and free African-descended populations. The painting thus functions as a visual document of daily life, leisure practices, and cultural expression within the plantation economy of late 18th-century South Carolina. The scene is not a religious scene, allegory, casta painting, or individual portrait, but rather a costumbrista (genre) scene depicting secular communal activity. No identifiable saint, allegorical figure, or hierarchical racial classification scheme is present. The composition does not include a donor figure or patron portrait.
